sections.html:
Up in the north of the state, Ouachita Parish is anchored by Monroe, its seat and biggest municipality, with West Monroe facing it across the Ouachita River. Those two are the only cities. Richwood and Sterlington are the towns. The 2020 census counted 160,368 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 158,542. Unincorporated communities that show up on property records include Bawcomville, Brownsville, Calhoun, Claiborne, Lakeshore and Swartz.

The housing stock reflects several growth waves, the first tied to the natural gas field found in 1916. Whatever decade your house comes from, buyers will quiz you on roof, wiring and plumbing. School district follows the address, with the Monroe City School System inside Monroe and the Ouachita Parish School Board elsewhere, so confirm yours before you describe schools to anyone.

Think of it as a hand-off: the Assessor decides what the property is worth, then the Sheriff collects. State law sets the outline and the Tax Commission writes assessment rules, while the police jury, school board and similar bodies pick the levies printed on your bill.

OfficeRoleHow to reach it
Ouachita Parish AssessorValues all taxable property and tracks homestead exemptionsRecords searchable online
Ouachita Parish Sheriff, Civil/Tax OfficeCollects as ex-officio tax collector(318) 324-2536; pay by mail, in person or online
Board of ReviewFirst appeal step after the AssessorDates come from the Assessor
Louisiana Tax CommissionSecond appeal stepState agency

Useful websites: opassessor.com offers a property search, an interactive map, millage rates by ward and a tax calculator, and opso.net carries the Sheriff's tax information.

Your tax starts with fair market value times a percentage fixed by law. Land and residential improvements both come in at 10 percent. Commercial property and personal property are assessed at 15 percent, except commercial land, which stays at 10 percent.

The maximum homestead exemption, $7,500, is subtracted from assessed value before millage is applied. City taxes are not reduced by it, which is why a house in Monroe or West Monroe can have a bigger total bill than a similar one outside the city limits.

A reassessment is required at least every four years, and a sale or change to the property can trigger one sooner. New buyers are asked to fill out a Sales Questionnaire, which the Assessor uses to check fair market value.

Under the general state rule, December brings the bill and December 31 is the deadline. Late balances add 1 percent interest per month. The Sheriff's Tax Office accepts mail, walk-in and online payments.

If the notice never reached you, you still owe the tax. Contact the tax collector for the amount.

  • One mailing per year, in December.
  • Interest on late balances: 1 percent a month.
  • Unpaid property may go to a tax sale. For immovable property sold that way, the debtor has three years to redeem.
  • Foreclosure and seizure sales belong to the Sheriff's Civil Division, which auctions on Wednesday mornings at 10 a.m. on an online platform.

Your first stop is the Assessor. The ladder after that runs from the Ouachita Parish Board of Review to the Louisiana Tax Commission to the courts.

Show proof that the value is off. Boards in Louisiana typically accept recent sale prices, an appraisal or photographs of damage. Outside Orleans Parish the tax roll is open for public inspection from August 15 to September 15. Miss the window and you usually wait a year.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption and the age freeze
sections.html:
Two breaks matter most: the homestead exemption and the assessment freeze for older owners. The exemption takes $7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of market value) off an owner-occupied home and can reach up to 160 acres containing the residence.

The Assessor's website has an application postcard and a page on the Special Assessment Value Freeze for owners 65 and older. A disability rating of at least 50 percent that is service connected can also qualify, within an income limit. Both benefits belong to the person living in the home, so whoever buys must apply on their own.

sections.h2: When a seizure or foreclosure is involved
sections.html:
Sheriff sales are public, and the Civil Division advertises each one in the legal section of a local newspaper before auction. The division handles writs of seizure and sale, garnishments, attachments and writs of possession. If a creditor has already moved against your house, the recorded seizure limits what a buyer can do, so talk to an attorney about timing before you sign a contract.

A seller who is behind on taxes, facing a seizure and carrying repairs often has more choices before the auction date than after it. Contact the Tax Office about the balance, then decide whether to list the house, sell it as-is for cash or work out a payment plan with the creditor.

sections.h2: What buyers will ask about your taxes
sections.html:
Expect three questions. Is the bill current? Does the homestead exemption or freeze stay with the house? What will the first bill look like after the sale? Your own exemption ends when you move out, and the new owner applies separately, so the first bill may be higher than yours. Having the last bill, the parcel number and the Assessor's property search page ready makes those answers quick.

A reassessment can follow a sale, which is another reason the Sales Questionnaire matters. Buyers who know this ahead of time are less likely to renegotiate late in the process. Share the exemption rules with them up front, including that the exemption does not reduce city taxes, and a house inside Monroe or West Monroe will not surprise anyone with its bill.

A tax debt attaches to the property, and it has to be cleared before clean title can pass. La. R.S. 47:1993 says the delivered assessment roll operates as a lien and privilege on every assessed property, usually ahead of other encumbrances.

Your closing attorney or title company requests a payoff from the Sheriff's Tax Office and settles it out of your proceeds. The deed is then recorded with the clerk of court on South Grand Street in Monroe. A house with a mortgage, back taxes and needed repairs makes for slower title work, so begin the payoff request early.

  1. Look up your parcel on the Assessor's site to check the owner and homestead status.
  2. Phone the Tax Office, (318) 324-2536, for the balance.
  3. Hand the title company that figure and any survey.
  4. At the table, the balance is deducted and the deed is sent for recording.

Any error you spot in the first step is cheaper to fix before the buyer's side finds it.

faqs.q: When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?
faqs.a: The general Louisiana rule is December 31, and late balances accrue 1 percent interest per month. Call the Sheriff's Tax Office at (318) 324-2536 to confirm the deadline for your bill.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: The Ouachita Parish Sheriff, acting as ex-officio tax collector. You can pay by mail, in person or online through the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: What is the Ouachita Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It is $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of fair market value, on an owner-occupied home. It does not apply to city taxes.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Ouachita Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Meet with the Assessor, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

faqs.q: Do I owe property tax at closing in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes are a lien and must be cleared for clear title, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds. Your closing attorney or title company requests the figure from the Tax Office.
